toc.title: Do we become dependent on safety cues? So what?
The real question: are you building self-regulation?
"I need to feel better" versus "my nervous system needs more regulation"
We build safety, we don't turn it on
The process of safety versus safety medicine
An example: a client in panic

blocks.p: I want to talk about safety cues: what they are, how to help your clients notice them and savor them, and hopefully grow the ability to get a bit more unstuck. This is general thinking for general situations, and there could be plenty of times when it doesn't apply.
One of my international listeners, a therapist, sent me this question:

q: How do you teach clients about safety cues so they don't depend on them? I'm thinking about someone who may be afraid to leave the house alone, but who discovers that leaving with someone regulates his or her nervous system.

blocks.p: A quick recap first. In the Polyvagal Theory, safety cues are basically what provides a neuroception of safety to our autonomic nervous system, through the brainstem.

This is different for everybody. What's a cue of safety for me versus a cue of safety for somebody else could be wildly different. I love the smell of oranges. That's very much a cue of safety for me that helps ground me in my nervous system. Lemons too. Citrusy kinds of things. But this could be very different from me to the next person to the next, based on all kinds of factors. Individual history is maybe the biggest one. What's a cue of safety for me could actually be a cue of danger for somebody else, based on the context of something they went through.

There are also universal cues of safety that apply to all of us human beings. Not exactly the same cue for all of us, obviously, but things like gentle eye contact and vocal prosody are typically going to be cues of safety for everyone. We might feel uncomfortable receiving them. They'll be received as a cue of safety, but then maybe experienced as discomfort if we're not used to being in our safety state.
When it comes to potentially being dependent on safety cues, I want to ask: is it a safety cue, or is it a protective cue? I guess I'll call it that.
A safety cue brings you feelings of safety. It shifts you up your [polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) into your state of safety and social engagement.

A protective cue keeps you in defense, but it might bring a sense of protection. Maybe relief, though I don't think that's quite the right word for it. A protective cue maybe diminishes the intensity of your defensive state, but you still stay in the defensive state. That's different than safety.

So if someone is having difficulty leaving the house, they might feel protected with somebody else, but that doesn't mean they're actually accessing their safety state. That's a big difference. And when someone notices what brings them to safety, talking that out in therapy is going to be a big part of identifying what actually brings them there.

blocks.h: Do we become dependent on safety cues? So what?

blocks.p: The wording "safety cue dependency" interested me, so I want to take this in my own direction for a bit, and then I'll bring it back to the question. Do we become dependent on safety cues? And if we do, so what? They're safety cues. What does it matter?

Where it might matter is if that other person is your safety cue. Then we might be using them for our own benefit, or a kind of pseudo benefit. We might be using them as a tool, and that does not go along with being in your safe and social state, in my opinion. If you're in your safe and social state, I don't think you're going to be using somebody else as a tool so that you can leave the house.

That's going to come from desperation, of course. It comes from wanting, needing, to minimize the amount of pain you're in. It comes from needing to be functional, absolutely. But at some point, that may be done at somebody else's expense, and I can see that being a problem. That's just one scenario, but there could easily be scenarios where a dysregulated person becomes manipulative of another person in order to feel what seems like safety, or relief, or protection. But I wouldn't really call that a safety cue. To me, that's a diminishing of defensive energy, which is something, but it's not a safety cue.

Now take the smell of an orange. Could I become dependent on the smell of an orange in order to self-regulate, to climb to the top of my polyvagal ladder and feel safety? And if so, who cares? Maybe if it became like an addiction, if it was interfering with my basic functioning, then it would be a problem, sure. If I had to leave a therapy session to go sniff an orange in order to come back into the room and be effective, I could see that being a problem.

But what if we're just using safety cues to self-regulate? Isn't that kind of the whole point of safety cues, at least the self-regulative ones we have some control over, the things that anchor us in our safety system? What else would you use to get to your safe and social state?

These external cues are for our senses. I use my sense of smell, with the orange, to ground myself. In therapy, I'll often have a picture of nature on a screen, something I find on YouTube, and that helps ground people. It's a safety cue for my clients. They use their senses to climb to the top of the ladder, to safety. That's self-regulation. Isn't that a good thing?

We can even use top-down, internal cues, like telling ourselves, "Hey, we're amazing, and we can handle whatever the situation is," or doing some sort of cognitive reframe. That's kind of a safety cue too. I don't personally see an issue with that.

blocks.h: The real question: are you building self-regulation?

blocks.p: So if we do these things, is that becoming dependent on them? I don't necessarily think it is. The issue for me is: are we building our self-regulation or not?

If we have a menu of options that bring us to safety, and we use what's on our menu, which I think is a really good idea, is it building our self-regulation? Are we building up our independence, our ability to self-regulate? Are we actually building up our distress tolerance?

We all need safety cues. That's very normal. We're all going to use external and internal safety cues. That's not an issue. But are you actually building up your capacity to tolerate more distress and to self-regulate? That's what it comes down to.

blocks.h: "I need to feel better" versus "my nervous system needs more regulation"

blocks.p: Here's something you could ask yourself, or think about with your clients. It might be the difference between "I need to feel better" and "my autonomic nervous system needs more regulation." There's a different flavor to those two statements.

"I need to feel better" can easily turn into addiction, or relief seeking, or protection seeking. It can turn into situations where your basic functioning is at risk, or where you eventually, even unwittingly, manipulate somebody else as a tool for your own feelings of protection.

I compare this to a medicinal kind of mindset: we rely on a safety cue as a dose of medicine, or we rely on experts to tell us what to do to feel better, to make the feelings go away. I need to feel better. Make this stop. Make this go away. And we know from the Polyvagal Theory that story follows state: the thoughts in our mind follow the state our autonomic nervous system is in. "I need to feel better" can have a very panicky flavor. It could probably fall into any of the defensive states on the polyvagal ladder, but my mind goes to the panicky one: I need to make this go away. I need to make this stop.
Using safety cues at that point isn't necessarily bad, but I could see it becoming a dependence. It's used more as a coping skill, maybe. It doesn't sound like genuine self-regulation building.

"My autonomic nervous system needs more regulation" has more of an element of mindfulness to it. You're aware of the somatic part of yourself, as distinct from your conscious awareness. You're able to witness your somatic needs. You're able to notice that your thinking self may be out of alignment with your somatic self, and that these need to align, come back to baseline, come back to the present moment. It's an accurate description of what's happening, rather than a need to make it stop.
The catch is that you kind of have to have some safety activated already in order to have that kind of mindfulness.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.h: We build safety, we don't turn it on

blocks.p: So again: are we building self-regulation or not? Safety cues are not an antidote to make defensive feelings go away. That's maybe coping at best. That's dealing with the moment and getting through it, and that's not bad. I'm not knocking anyone for it. You do what you've got to do to get through the moment. But ideally, we want to build the capacity to self-regulate.
We build safety. It's not something we turn on by smelling an orange. In that moment, it can be grounding, but does it help you build self-regulation overall?

The idea is to identify what brings you to safety, and not just identify it, but incorporate it more into your system, especially mindfully: mindfully practicing what brings you to safety, and building the capacity to actually stay in your safety state. That's absolutely essential for building safety. And over time, in general, the need to do something like smelling an orange, or being with someone to get out of the house, should decrease. If you just practice it, every day or even weekly, the need to do a grounding skill should decrease over time.

blocks.h: The process of safety versus safety medicine

blocks.p: Here's a reframe, especially for my fellow therapists. With our clients, we want to frame this as a process of building the capacity to self-regulate. Safety cues are not medicine. They're not a dose of something to get you through the moment. Well, they can be, but overall they're more than that. It's not a pill we take to feel better. The process of safety is more than coping with the present moment and applying a dose of safety cue medicine. It's a process we have to build. We have to exercise the capacity to feel safe.
Safety medicine is, "Here's your cue of safety, and hopefully it'll help you out." The process of safety has three parts:

ol: Teaching. In session, we teach about these things. For example, we can teach about fidgets.
Experiencing. We guide our clients in experiencing safety in session, for example through fidgeting, with their feedback, making adjustments as we need to.

Developing. We send them home with homework to develop their safety sensations: using fidgets they might have at home, or getting curious about and identifying new things at home that help them feel safety.

blocks.p: So it's not just one thing. It's an ongoing, longer process of safety. And the whole time, our clients are mindfully experiencing safety and what that feels like.

blocks.h: An example: a client in panic

blocks.p: I had a session with a teen client who came in in a pretty panicked state. She wasn't able to talk about why, and actually didn't want to. She said, "No, I'm not going to go into it." Okay, fine. So we just had to deal with the present moment and the panicky feelings. No problem solving, nothing like that. Just the somatic pieces.

I have fidgets in my office, so I had them ready to go. I had nature on the screen. For this session in particular, it was a ten-hour YouTube video of forest scenes that changed every ten minutes or so to a different location in the forest. I was checking in with her about her breathing consistently through the session, and about the sensations she was having in her body in the present moment.

As she looked at the nature on the screen, I would prompt her: "How do you feel about this? If you were there, what would you be up to right now?" She would use her imagination to say what she'd be up to and who was there with her. As the scene changed, I'd ask again: "How do you feel about this one? Who's there with you now?"
So we used her imagination, the physical fidgeting, breath check-ins, and consciously slowing down her breathing when we were able to. All these different things to help her ground herself in safety.

Any of those pieces can be helpful in the moment of a panic attack. But we also had pieces she could take, practice, and develop further on her own, at home or even in class. You can do deep breathing in class. You can notice your somatic sensations in class.

During this whole process, we were noticing the process of accessing safety. It's not all at once. It's not like I gave her her safety cue medicine and she was good. Over that sixty-minute session, we were able to see what helped her feel more or less safe, and that's just for that hour. Over the weeks she was in therapy, she was able to see, week after week, what helped her come to safety and stay in safety. And she could see, "Oh, my defensive, panicky, anxious feelings are decreasing week after week after week."

That growth is often missed, but it needs to be talked about in therapy. We should be checking in about goals and how things are going: are symptoms reduced, increased, staying the same? We should be tracking progress, so that week after week we can see a long process, or maybe even a short one, of getting more and more self-regulated.

When clients share their experience of safety with us, it makes it more real, in a way. It's not just in their mind, and it's not just in their body. Now they're actually sharing it out loud with a trusted person, us as their therapist.

And when you share something like that with somebody who understands, who's listening, who takes you seriously and can have empathy for you, who takes your feelings, thoughts, and sensations seriously and validates them, normalizes them, and encourages them, that's a much different experience than you get elsewhere outside of therapy.
That mindfulness, and sharing it with somebody, is a big part of the process of building safety, and not just receiving safety cue medicine.

Whether you're a therapist or a client, think about what helps you come to safety. Is it something you're trying to do to turn safety on? Or is it a process you're letting unfold? Become curious about that journey, that process of becoming more and more grounded in your safety state.
